AnisoMamba-Reg: Anisotropy-Aware Scan Ordering for Cardiac Cine MRI Deformable Registration

Min Sung Lee

Master’s thesis, Department of Information Convergence Engineering (AI Major), Pusan National University

Advisor: Prof. Jin Kyu Gahm, School of Computer Science and Engineering

OverviewMotivationMethodExperimentsResultsAblationConclusionResourcesReferences

Overview

Aligning the end-diastolic (ED) and end-systolic (ES) frames of a cardiac cine MRI is a basic step for estimating myocardial strain, checking wall motion, and measuring cardiac function. This thesis presents AnisoMamba-Reg, an unsupervised deformable registration network built on Mamba, a selective state-space model that reads 3D features as a 1D sequence.

The order in which that sequence is read decides which voxels end up as neighbors. Cardiac MRI is strongly anisotropic (1.8 × 1.8 × 10.0 mm), so we redesign the scan order around that fact instead of treating all three axes alike.

Contributions

  • An anisotropic patch embedding and a Siamese Mamba encoder that combines the two images' features by sum and difference.
  • A scan ordering that reads in-plane (H, W) tokens first: HWD and WHD permutations, each traversed forward and in reverse (four paths, called Flip4-scan).
  • A Laplacian-pyramid decoder with feature warping (adopted from LapWarp), combined with these encoder features, followed by velocity-field integration.
Motivation →

Motivation

Why ED–ES registration matters

The deformation field from ED to ES is the starting point for strain estimation, regional wall-motion analysis, and other measures of cardiac function [1, 2]. Errors in the field carry over into these measurements, for example when judging functional recovery after myocardial infarction or telling apart conditions such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

The task is demanding. ED and ES differ by a large deformation, contraction (ED→ES) and relaxation (ES→ED) are not equally hard, and the network has to capture both the global change of shape and local changes at tissue boundaries.

Mamba and the order of the sequence

CNN-based registration has a limited receptive field, and Transformer-based registration becomes expensive as the number of tokens grows. Mamba models long-range dependencies efficiently, but it processes a 1D sequence. A 3D feature map therefore has to be flattened, and the flattening order determines which voxels are neighbors in the sequence.

Cardiac MRI is anisotropic

Cine MRI is acquired as thick short-axis slices. After resampling, the in-plane spacing is 1.8 mm and the slice spacing is 10.0 mm, about 5.6 times coarser. If the feature map is flattened without a scan-order design, tokens that are adjacent along the depth axis (D) are also adjacent in the sequence, and the relationship along D may be weighted more strongly than the in-plane structure.

Can anisotropy-aware scan ordering improve Mamba-based cardiac deformable registration?

← OverviewMethod →

Method

AnisoMamba-Reg takes a moving and a fixed volume (128 × 128 × 16) and predicts the deformation that warps the moving volume onto the fixed one (Figure 1). It has four parts: an encoder, feature fusion, a decoder, and a registration head.

Anisotropic Siamese Mamba encoder

  • Anisotropic patch embedding. A (4, 4, 1) kernel and stride shrink H and W by 4 and keep all 16 slices: 128×128×16 becomes 32×32×16 with 96 channels.
  • Three stages with 96, 192, and 384 channels (depths 2, 2, 4). Patch merging between stages is 2×2×1, so the slice axis is never merged.
  • Siamese weights. The moving and fixed volumes go through the same encoder independently.
  • Feature fusion. At each stage the two feature maps are summed and subtracted, and the results are concatenated (192, 384, 768 channels). The sum carries what the two images share and the difference carries how they differ.

Scan ordering

Each AnisoMamba block normalizes its input and passes it through four parallel Mamba (SSM) branches, one per scan path. The branch outputs are summed and added to the input through a residual connection:

xout = x + Σk=14 SSMk( LN( x ) )

LN is layer normalization. The four paths are HWD and WHD, each forward and reverse. In this notation D (depth) comes last, so every path sweeps the H–W plane of a slice before moving to the next slice; HWD and WHD differ in which in-plane axis is swept first. The left panel of Figure 3 shows the conventional order, in which tokens along D sit next to each other.

Decoder and registration head

  • A four-level Laplacian pyramid predicts a residual displacement at each resolution and accumulates it from coarse to fine. When the accumulated field is upsampled, displacements are doubled in H and W only.
  • Feature warping at the 1/8 and 1/4 resolutions: the moving features are warped with the field accumulated so far, and the sum and difference with the fixed features are recomputed (technique from LapWarp).
  • A 3×3 convolution with tanh gives a velocity field, which VecInt integrates with 7 scaling-and-squaring steps. Adding the upsampled pyramid displacement gives the final deformation, and a spatial transformer (STN) warps the moving image.

Training objective (unsupervised)

L = LNCC + 0.1·Lgrad + 0.5·Lms + 1.0·LIC + 1.0·LJP

  • NCC: local normalized cross-correlation between the warped moving image and the fixed image.
  • grad: smoothness of the velocity field.
  • ms: NCC at each pyramid level.
  • IC: consistency between the forward and backward velocity fields.
  • JP: Jacobian penalty, mean[max(−det J, 0)2], which penalizes only folded voxels.
← MotivationExperiments →

Experiments

Data

We use ACDC [16], which provides ED and ES cine MRI volumes with left-ventricle (LV), right-ventricle (RV), and myocardium (Myo) labels. Volumes are resampled with SimpleITK to 1.8 × 1.8 × 10.0 mm and cropped or padded to 128 × 128 × 16. The network is trained on images only; labels are used for evaluation.

Training

  • Adam optimizer, initial learning rate 1×10−4, batch size 1, 500 epochs with 10 steps per epoch.
  • Random horizontal and vertical flips; both ES→ED and ED→ES pairs are used.
  • 5-fold cross-validation (80 training and 20 validation subjects per fold). The checkpoint with the highest validation bidirectional Dice is kept for each fold.
  • The 50 held-out test subjects are used for all reported results. For the final model, the deformation fields of the five fold models are averaged voxel by voxel (flow averaging) before warping.

Metrics

  • Dice: mean over LV, RV, and Myo, averaged over ES→ED and ED→ES (bidirectional Dice).
  • HD95: 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance in mm.
  • NJD: percentage of voxels with a non-positive Jacobian determinant (folding).
  • SDlogJ: standard deviation of log det J, a measure of how much the local volume change varies.

Compared methods

VoxelMorph, TransMorph, MambaMorph, and LapWarp, the memory-free variant of MemWarp. VoxelMorph, TransMorph, and MambaMorph were proposed for other domains and were retrained here with the same protocol.

Results

Table 1. Comparison on the ACDC test set (50 subjects).
MethodAvg Dice (%)LVRVMyoHD95 (mm)NJD (%)SDlogJ
VoxelMorph74.5679.9772.6071.119.370.0000.0344
TransMorph75.3480.5673.3372.139.300.0000.0347

MambaMorph74.1278.8872.7670.739.600.0000.0402
AnisoMamba-Reg (ours)79.7284.1677.4677.538.290.0990.0658

Dice is the mean of LV, RV, and Myo over both directions. AnisoMamba-Reg uses the 5-fold flow-averaging ensemble; its single-model result (Flip4-scan) is 79.21% Dice, see Ablation.

  • Accuracy. AnisoMamba-Reg has the highest Dice and the lowest HD95. It is 2.51 points above LapWarp and 5.60 points above MambaMorph, which also uses a Mamba backbone.
  • Folding. NJD is 0.099%, lower than LapWarp (0.156%). VoxelMorph, TransMorph, and MambaMorph show no folding, but their Dice is lower.
  • Deformation spread. LapWarp and AnisoMamba-Reg have nearly the same SDlogJ (0.0660 and 0.0658), higher than the other three (0.03–0.04). Those three also have the lowest Dice, which may indicate more conservative deformations.

Qualitative comparison

In this case AnisoMamba-Reg aligns the RV boundary closest to the fixed segmentation. LapWarp shows several folded regions around the LV boundary, and the proposed method shows a smaller one, which matches the NJD values in Table 1. This is a single example chosen for illustration.

← ExperimentsAblation →

Scan-order ablation

All rows use the same network and training; only the scan paths change. The baseline is the conventional flattening order (DHW), in which tokens along depth are adjacent. These are single-model results, so Flip4-scan is 79.21% here, and the 79.72% in Table 1 adds the 5-fold ensemble.

Table 2. Scan-order ablation (single model, no ensemble). F/R = forward/reverse traversal.
ConfigurationScan orderAvg Dice (%)Gain over baselineHD95 (mm)NJD (%)SDlogJ
BaselineDHW78.03+0.008.870.2030.076
1-scanHWD78.83+0.808.500.1480.069
2-scanHWD, WHD78.98+0.958.430.1550.081
4-scanHWD, WHD, DHW, DWH78.89+0.868.570.1460.075
6-scanHWD-F/R, WHD-F/R, DHW-F/R78.91+0.888.560.1430.072
Flip4-scanHWD-F/R, WHD-F/R79.21+1.188.410.1420.072
  • Reading in-plane first helps. Replacing the baseline with a single HWD path raises Dice from 78.03% to 78.83%, and adding the WHD path gives 78.98%.
  • More paths are not better. Adding depth-adjacent paths lowers Dice: 4-scan (78.89%) is below 2-scan (78.98%), and 6-scan (78.91%) is below Flip4-scan (79.21%). The 6-scan configuration is Flip4-scan plus DHW forward and reverse.
  • Flip4-scan is best. It has the highest Dice (79.21%) and the lowest NJD (0.142%) among the six configurations. SDlogJ is lowest for 1-scan (0.069), so the deformation spread does not follow a single trend.
← ResultsConclusion →

Conclusion

Findings

  • Taking the anisotropy of cardiac MRI into account when ordering the Mamba scan improved registration accuracy.
  • Flip4-scan (HWD and WHD, forward and reverse) was the best of the scan configurations tested.
  • AnisoMamba-Reg reached 79.72% bidirectional Dice and 8.29 mm HD95 on ACDC.

Limitations

  • Some folding remains (NJD 0.099%), mostly in strongly deformed regions such as the ventricular boundaries.
  • The ablation covers the scan strategy only; the other components were not ablated individually.
  • The final result uses a 5-fold ensemble, and all experiments use one dataset (ACDC).

Future work

Stronger regularization of the deformation field in highly deformed regions, and extensions of the scan strategy.
